The house was not built for spectacle.
It was built for coming back.

In 1916, those were saplings. Now they are a forest.

1915 TO 1916

Built for Walter Hines Page, ambassador to the Court of St James’s.

Planned from London, letter by letter, while the war kept him there.

The same craftsmen who built Pinehurst built this house.

The full history, documented  →

ACT II

The house, in living order.

A walk from the front door to the back garden, in the order the rooms were built to be used.

THE ENTRY

A door that has been open since 1916.

Step through. The brick was laid by the same hands that laid the rest of Pinehurst. The light at the end of the hall is the same one Page wrote home about.

Flemish bond brick. A water table.

THE LIVING ROOM

A long, quiet room. The mantel has always been lit in winter.

So is the brass hardware on every door. The proportions belong to 1916 and have not been argued with since.

Original oak flooring. Brass key plates still in the locks.

THE LIVING ROOM

The heart of the first floor.

A room built for conversation after dinner. The French doors are not decoration. They are the way out.

The room. And then, the air.

THE SITTING ROOM

A small room, painted in blue and white, with a stair that turns back on itself.

The winder stair is the kind of detail a builder only puts in when the owner is not looking. It has been here a century.

From the tiles to the spiral. The stair does not apologize for itself.

THE DINING ROOM

The room Page intended for long, slow nights.

The frontispiece and the leaded glass sidelights survived the 1999 restoration without being touched. The mantel did too.

Original frontispiece, leaded glass sidelights, an over-door fanlight. Seven mantels in the house. This is the second.

THE LIBRARY

Page was an editor. The room remembers it.

Floor to ceiling shelves in three walls. A writing desk by the window. A mantel that has been the third of seven.

THE KITCHEN

The one room that is not 1916. And the one that earned the most care.

The kitchen is original to the 1999 to 2001 restoration. The pre-restoration kitchen lived in the basement. This one looks out over the boxwood garden, which is the only thing on the property that the cooks can see from the stove.

Reclaimed heart pine floors. The only room in the house that does not have the original oak.

From the cook’s eye, the garden. The kitchen ends where the boxwood begins.

THE BUTLER’S PANTRY

A working room, kept exactly as it was.

The passage between the kitchen and the dining room. The silver lives here. So does the quiet before dinner.

THE POWDER ROOM

The jewel box.

Two small rooms, papered in pattern. Both are original to the restoration. Neither is large enough to sit down in. That is the point.

A pedestal sink. A skirted vanity. Toile and botanical wallpaper. The smallest rooms get the most care.

THE PRIMARY SUITE

The fourth mantel. The quietest corner of the second floor.

A wide room with the proportions of a 1916 bedroom. The bath sits behind a curving bay. The dressing rooms run on either side.

The house does not reveal itself all at once.

ACT IV

Upstairs, briefly.

Three suites and a den. The second floor is where the family lived when the family still lived here.

THE ROSE SUITE

A bedroom painted in the color of its name.

THE YELLOW SUITE

Two beds and a Wedgwood shelf. The balcony is right there.

THE RED BEDROOM

The nursery. The brass bed. The rocking horse is not for sale.

THE DEN

Up the winder. A room that closes the second floor in on itself.

ACT VI

The grounds.

Four acres of the original thousand. Pine, boxwood, brick, a pool in a walled garden, and two courts waiting for new paint.

Four point one five acres. The original house parcel, intact.

TWO COURTS

Two lighted courts. They ask for new surfaces and nothing more.

Regulation, fenced, lit. Built for play. The only honesty is the surface. The new owner picks the date and the paint.

ACT VII

The plans.

Drawn for the 1999 to 2001 restoration by Thomas O’Shea, architect. Fifteen sheets transfer with the property.

ACT VIII

The last of the original parcel.

The land was sold in pieces. The house was not.

A subdivision rose around it and carries the name still. The house kept the rest: the brick, the forest, the four acres that were always its own.

Offered now.
